Affaire Kalubi: deux policiers cités à c: Kalubi Case: Two Police Officers Summoned to Appear Before Police Ethics Committee
Le soir de son arrestation, David revena: On the night of his arrest, David was coming home from an evening with friends.
Dominic Gagné et Mathieu Paré, deux agen: Dominic Gagné and Mathieu Paré, two officers with the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM), must answer four counts in a citation before the Comité de déontologie policière (Police Ethics Committee) in a case dating back three years. The news may provide answers to the questions David Tshiteya Kalubi’s family has been asking.
Le 8 novembre 2017, David Tshiteya Kalub: On November 8, 2017, David Tshiteya Kalubi <l1>died at the Montréal municipal court</l1>. The 23-year-old had been arrested by the SPVM the day before, at 10:40 p.m. He spent the night in detention at the Centre opérationnel Est before being transferred to a cell at the municipal court around 7:35 a.m. At 8:45 a.m., he was found unresponsive in his cell. He was pronounced dead at the Centre hospitalier universitaire de Montréal at 9:53 a.m.
Le Comité déterminera si les agents ont: The Committee will determine whether the officers failed in their duty by showing negligence or recklessness with regard to Mr. Kalubi’s health. The hearing date has not yet been set, and the SPVM confirmed to us that the two officers summoned are still in its employ.
« Les trois dernières années n’ont pas é: “The last three years haven’t been easy,” confides Quelyna Kalubi, the deceased’s older sister. “Life was turned upside down for the whole family, especially for my mother, who blames herself for not being there,” she adds. On the night of November 7, 2017, Ms. Tshiteya, a nurse, was in Gatineau, where she was working. Around 10 p.m., after an evening out, her son David set out for home. One of his friends was driving. He would never reach his destination. Police stopped the two young men at a traffic check. Two outstanding arrest warrants that had not been endorsed were on Mr. Kalubi’s file, and the officers proceeded to arrest him.
« Ce n’était pas quelqu'un d’arrogant ou: “He wasn’t arrogant or proud,” says Quelyna of her younger brother. “He never missed a chance to help you or tell you he loved you.” David Kalubi suffered from sickle cell anemia, a serious chronic disease his sister knows well, since she also has it. This genetic disease, which affects almost exclusively Black populations, causes red blood cells to be misshapen, and the complications can be fatal.
« Nous, on nous a dit que David était mo: “We were told David died of natural causes, when he was anemic,” says Quelyna. “It only takes an hour or two of treatment to restore the hemoglobin level and hydrate a sick person.”
Elle croit que s’il avait été à l’hôpita: She believes that if he had been in hospital at that moment, he could have been saved. The symptoms of sickle cell anemia can vary from one person to another, and the crises are sometimes extremely painful.
« On compare les crises vaso-occlusives: “People compare vaso-occlusive crises to what a woman in labour feels,” says Quelyna, whose two-and-a-half-year-old son bears his uncle’s name. Sickle cell anemia can lead to organ failure, and heart and brain problems are common among those who have it. David’s heart problems, diagnosed shortly before the tragedy, were known to his family.
« Mon père a la même maladie, et il a 70: “My father has the same disease, and he’s 70.” He is also a cardiologist. “That’s no reason to say David died because he had heart problems,” Quelyna believes. However, according to the coroner’s analysis, the fact that the young man had not taken his medication for 24 hours had no bearing on his death. His death is instead attributed to the presence of cocaine in his blood and its effect on his heart. A conclusion that leaves the Kalubi family perplexed.
Le soir de son arrestation, David revena: On the night of his arrest, David was coming home from an evening with friends. He wasn’t feeling well and had decided to go home to take his medication, his sister says. He was a few minutes from his home, in Hochelaga. Mr. Kalubi reportedly told the police about his health condition. He also reportedly told them he didn’t have his medication and wanted to go get it, a fact confirmed by the investigation report of the Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes (BEI). Information gathered during the investigation reveals that the officers asked David Kalubi no further questions when he mentioned his health condition and said he was taking medication.
On apprend aussi que l’état de santé du: We also learn that the young man’s health condition is not mentioned in the police reports. The officers refused to let David go get his medication, and he spent the night in detention at the SPVM’s Centre opérationnel Est before being transferred to the municipal court. These decisions violate police ethics, but do not make the officers criminally responsible for Mr. Kalubi’s death, according to the Director of Criminal and Penal Prosecutions (DPCP).
Mais pourquoi donc faire passer les agen: So why bring Officers Gagné and Paré, who drove David Kalubi to the Centre opérationnel after his arrest, before the Police Ethics Committee?
D’après le Commissaire, le jour de l’arr: According to the Commissioner, on the day of the arrest, officers 6129 and 6299 were negligent or reckless with regard to Mr. Kalubi’s health and safety, notably by failing to fill out the detainee monitoring form, which assesses a detainee’s health. Furthermore, according to the Commissioner, after the incident, Officer Gagné made a false statement in the police report dated November 16, 2017, a week after Mr. Kalubi’s death. Officer Paré did the same during the BEI investigation on January 16, 2018, again according to the Commissioner. Contacted by La Converse, the DPCP declined to comment on the citations.
Face à ces faits, Alexandre Popovic, de: Given these facts, Alexandre Popovic of the Coalition contre la répression et les abus policiers (CRAP), who filed the police ethics complaint, questions the relevance of the DPCP’s report and of the system of sanctions against police abuse. “The allegations in the citation are acts that can amount to a criminal offence,” he says. “We’re talking about medical negligence while in police custody. David Kalubi’s case makes me think of Joyce Echaquan’s.”
<strong>La déontologie, un recours pour: Is police ethics a recourse for victims’ families?
À la suite d’un incident, ou de la conna: After an incident, or after learning of one, a complainant has one year to file a police ethics complaint. In Mr. Kalubi’s case, the complaint was filed on December 27, 2017, by a third party, Alexandre Popovic. The Kalubi family was not aware of the proceedings Mr. Popovic had launched until we called. Quelyna explains that the ethics process had been mentioned, but that at the time, the grieving family was not in a position to make a decision. She believes they were informed more than a year after her brother’s death.
La secrétaire générale et responsable de: Marie-Ève Bilodeau, secretary general and head of prevention at the offices of the Commissaire à la déontologie policière, believes a change is needed in this regard. “We’ve asked that the BEI systematically inform individuals and families that there is a recourse in police ethics, and that they shouldn’t wait until the investigation is over, because by then it’s often too late,” she says. “Often there’s a lack of awareness, especially when it involves immigrants or people who know little about their recourses. We’re very aware that there’s a problem.” The Commissioner cannot know whether its recommendations have been implemented. The Commissioner’s office has asked the Comité consultatif sur la réalité policière for more resources to better inform people about their recourses and to do prevention work with police officers.
Pour que des procédures en déontologie s: For police ethics proceedings to begin, the criminal investigation must be complete. “The Police Ethics Commissioner will first wait for the results of the independent investigation and see whether there will be criminal charges,” explains Mr. Popovic. Criminal proceedings take precedence over ethics proceedings, which could explain the delay between the filing of the complaint and the officers being summoned.
Si le DPCP juge que les agents ne sont p: If the DPCP finds that the officers are not responsible, the Police Ethics Commissioner may still draw different conclusions. Ms. Bilodeau explains the difference this way: “The BEI looks at criminal law, whereas police ethics concerns the code of ethics.”
Par exemple, lorsque des accusations cri: For example, when criminal charges are laid, ethics charges are automatically laid as well. The Police Ethics Committee is an administrative tribunal where the Commissioner, who acts on behalf of the complainant, must prove that the officer’s conduct was in breach of the code. “He’s not the client’s lawyer, he’s the prosecutor,” says the secretary general. “He makes sure to build a case and establish proof of an officer’s misconduct. He’s the one who determines the misconduct and which article of the Code of Ethics was breached.”
Lorsqu’on parle de citations, comme cell: In the case of citations, like those Officers Paré and Gagné face, the Commissioner lists the officers’ breaches in a document and cites the articles that were violated. The file is then submitted to a committee. As in a trial, the officer is entitled to a lawyer and must present a defence. Sanctions can range from a reprimand to dismissal of the officer.
La décision du Comité de déontologie ser: Will the Police Ethics Committee’s decision be a balm for the Kalubis’ wounds? Quelyna hopes justice will be done. “It’s good that other people understood our pain and are trying to get justice for someone who can’t do it himself, because we don’t have the strength,” she says. “We thought we were the only ones thinking about him, but I see there are other people.”
La soeur du défunt se rappelle en outre: The deceased’s sister also recalls that the results of the BEI investigation had surprised the family. “And when we got the DPCP’s decision, two years after the events, we didn’t know what to do,” she says. “We weren’t allowed to see the video, and the officers who were there that night refused to testify on their lawyer’s advice.”
La famille n’a pas non plus été en mesur: The family was also unable to see David’s body until it was laid out for viewing. “It’s as if they’re blaming the dead man for his own death,” she says sadly. “We’re told he should have taken his medication, he should have had it with him, he should have worn a bracelet – when there’s no bracelet for sickle cell anemia.”
Dans le cas d’un décès ou de blessures g: In the event of a death or serious injury occurring during a police intervention or while in detention, the Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes (BEI), a specialized police force, automatically conducts an investigation to shed light on the events.
Une fois l’enquête terminée, le dossier: Once the investigation is complete, the file is sent to the Director of Criminal and Penal Prosecutions (DPCP), an independent prosecution service answerable to the provincial government, which can act as prosecutor to defend the interests of the public and of victims in the case of a criminal act.
Depuis sa création, en 2016, le BEI a me: Since its creation in 2016, the BEI has conducted 181 independent investigations following deaths or injuries. No charges have been laid against police officers.
Le rapport annuel 2019-2020 du Commissai: The 2019-2020 annual report of the Police Ethics Commissioner reports 2,000 complaints processed, 179 investigations conducted and 90 officers cited during the period covered. 5
